tagline: From southern pine forests to the sharp turns of the Ozarks
intro: Scenic 7 runs from Arkansas’s southern border near El Dorado to Harrison, crossing pine and cypress country, the Ouachitas, the Arkansas River Valley and the Ozarks. The road snakes through the Ouachita National Forest and turns sharply in the Ozarks. The Forest Service identifies its national forest scenic byway sections with mountain scenery and fall color. Arkansas Tourism describes a journey through four geographic regions, from coastal-plain forests to mountain ridgelines, with farmland between the two mountain regions.

Two earlier state roads formed a rough predecessor to the present route when it appeared as a state-maintained road in 1924. The state numbered Highway 7 in 1926. Its scenic identity came later: in 1993, the Arkadelphia-to-Harrison section became Arkansas’s first scenic byway. An extension in 1999 brought the southern section from the Louisiana line into the byway. Highway 7 continues beyond Harrison to Diamond City, but that northern stretch lies outside the scenic designation.

Driving north, pass El Dorado and Camden before reaching the Ouachita foothills near Arkadelphia. At Hot Springs, the highway passes directly in front of Bathhouse Row. Beyond the forest, the route enters farmland and woodlands in the Arkansas River Valley at Dardanelle and Russellville. It then climbs into the Ozarks, passes the Grand Canyon of the Ozarks vista before Jasper, and finishes at Harrison.

moments.title: Bathhouse Row
moments.text: Eight bathhouses face the highway in Hot Springs, but these are later generations of buildings, not the structures of 1832. That year, the federal government set aside the hot springs and their area of origin. The row’s separate businesses competed for bathers; their architecture mixed neoclassical, Renaissance Revival, Spanish and Italianate styles. Covering Hot Springs Creek with a masonry arch in 1884 removed the need for individual bridges to the bathhouses and made room for gardens. Bronze eagles on stone pillars mark the old main entrance between the Maurice and Fordyce buildings.
moments.notice: Two bronze eagles on stone pillars flank the old entrance between the Maurice and Fordyce bathhouses.

moments.title: Grand Canyon of the Ozarks
moments.text: South of Jasper, Scenic 7 bends beside the vista Arkansas Tourism calls the Grand Canyon of the Ozarks. The agency describes this section as sharply twisting and popular with motorcyclists. Rugged ridgelines in the Ozark National Forest dominate the drive here. Beyond the vista, the northbound road reaches Jasper’s small town square near the Buffalo National River.

moments.title: Harrison
moments.text: Harrison’s downtown square marks the northern end of the scenic byway. Arkansas Tourism describes old brick storefronts with awnings and hanging flower baskets, anchored by the Boone County Courthouse and the restored Hotel Seville. Architect Charles L. Thompson designed the courthouse as a two-story brick building in Georgian Revival style. Bands of cast stone mark its floor levels, and the projecting entrance has brick pilasters and a bullseye window in its gable. Highway 7 carries on north, but Harrison is where its scenic designation ends. The courthouse remains in use at the center of the square.
